new_statements.translation: 5.1. The result of the morphological analysis seems to indicate that the position of the accent depends above all on the morphemic structure of Bubi. 5.2. In reduplicated forms the accent of the simple form is kept: /nkundákunda/ 'heels', /itumbátumbe/ 'clouds', /milukáluka/ 'scorpions', /mulámendemende/ 'livers'. 5.3. Accent is not automatic in the Bubi language. Secondary accent exists: /bubálè/ 'stone', /matálè/ 'stones'. [...] 6.4. [A problem requiring further study is] the tonal system, in which two different tones are clearly distinguished: /poto/ 'deity' vs /potó/ 'thanks', /sokó/ 'note' vs /sokó/ 'drumstick'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Bubi is a two-tone (H/L) Bantu language (Levin 1965 sec. 6.4; Bolekia 2008: 77, 2009: 11). The only explicit modern accent statement (Levin 1965, Batete dialect) says word accent is not positionally automatic: its place is governed mainly by morphemic structure (the accent sits on the stem, e.g. it stays on the base in reduplications), i.e. not a fixed-syllable rule. The 19th-c. missionary Clarke (1848: 10-11) heard accent 'usually on the penultimate' with a second accent on the first syllable of four-syllable words; Juanola (1890: 13-14) heard oxytone, paroxytone and proparoxytone words and 'an accent on every syllable' in some. Bolekia's modern descriptions give no stress rule at all and treat prominence purely as H vs L tone.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Levin 1965: 'Existe el acento secundario: /bubálè/, /matálè/' (grave accent marks the secondary). Clarke 1848: four-syllable words have accent on the first as well as the penultimate syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: Levin: reduplicated forms keep the accent of the simple form. Clarke: compound words and words with the 'double catching sound' (glottal stop) have a double accent.
new_statements.domain_note: Levin's data are isolated citation forms (nouns, numerals) from the Batete (south-western) dialect, impressionistic phonetics; his 'acento' marks very likely track stem high tone. Bolekia (2008: 77) notes word tone changes with syntactic position.
new_statements.identity_note: Levin 1965 describes the Batete dialect (south-west Bioko, near Luba/San Carlos), i.e. Glottolog's Southwest Bobe [sout2819]; Bolekia's works describe mainly north/north-western varieties (North Bobe [nort2804]); Clarke 1848 and Juanola 1890 are based on northern (Clarence/Santa Isabel, Banapá/Basupú) speech with appendices on Concepción and San Carlos. All are bube1242 Bube/Bubi of Bioko, not the Cameroonian Bubia/Wovea (bbx).

new_statements.translation: [p.25] Accordingly, Bubi has two level tones: a high (acute) one and a low (grave) one [...] [p.27] In Bubi the function of accent is differential. [...] In Bubi, words may carry one, two, three or more accents, with a culminative function in some cases or a distinctive function in others (distinguishing near-homonyms). [...] 1.4.2.1 Words without accent: those in which no syllable is pronounced with more force than another. [...] [p.28] 1.4.2.2 Words with accent: of several kinds, from those bearing a single accent to those bearing two, three or more: a) words with a single accent - on the final syllable: ré 'river', vötyó 'night' ... - on the penultimate syllable: bönánna 'old man', bötúkku 'chief' - on the antepenultimate syllable: ... ebilákobbe 'bunch of plantains' ... b) words with two, three or more accents (in all positions).

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for 'Bubi, Batete dialect' has an empty rule; the one existing statement (Levin 1965, Batete) says accent position depends mainly on morphemic structure and is kept in reduplication, i.e. not positionally fixed. Bolekia 1991 is compatible with that (no fixed position; accent lexical/distinctive, zero to several per word, co-described with a two-tone system) and adds detail: explicit two-tone analysis with minimal pairs, the classes accentless / single accent (final, penult, antepenult) / multiple accents, and phrase-level loss of word accent. It does not support any fixed-position reading. Note it is a pan-dialectal normative course, not a description of Batete specifical…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Bubi is described as a two-tone language (H/L, with rising and falling contours as combinations; tonal minimal pairs such as saala 'hunger' vs saalá 'palm-kernel shell'). 'Accent' is treated separately but has no fixed position: a word may have no accented syllable at all (level 0: nabba 'animal', botyo 'person', lokande, sipando), exactly one accent on the final, penultimate or antepenultimate syllable, or two or more accents in any positions (lötólló 'tongue', etómbátómbá 'fog'); its function is called 'differential'/distinctive, and misplacing it distorts the message; p. 22 speaks of 'la movilidad del acento en bubi'. The accented syllables are written with the same acute mark as high tone, and the 'accentless' words are the all-low-tone words of 1.4.1, so the author's 'accent' largely tracks lexical high tone rather than an independent, positionally fixed stress. Sec. 1.4.3: in connected speech word accent/tone may be lost or shifted 'en beneficio del grupo o frase'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No primary/secondary hierarchy is stated; words with 'two, three or more accents (in all positions)' are listed as a class of their own, without ranking the accents.
new_statements.exceptions: Words with no accent at all (monosyllables la, na, the augments ö, ë, i, a; disyllables nabba, bappa, botyo; trisyllables lokande, sipando, bösöppë; polysyllables enokonokko, erobasosso); loss of word accent and of gemination inside the phonic group (1.4.3, p. 29); loanwords are 'bubinizados' with class prefix and Bubi accent (p. 9) but no placement rule is given for them.
new_statements.identity_note: Bolekia 1991 is explicitly a unifying, normative course for Bubi as a whole: the prologue says it merges 'las tendencias dialectales más representativas, sin.. clasificar por zonas', and the text cites northern/north-eastern and southern/south-western forms side by side (e.g. bossö / botyo / mondyö 'person'); the author's own 1988 thesis is on north-eastern Bubi. It is therefore not a description of the Batete (south-western) dialect that the catalog item bube1242#rt1 and Levin 1965 name; its accent/tone statements are offered for the language generally.

sources.note: Sec. 5.3 'El tono' (pp. 77-79): Bubi has two level tones ('dos tonos puntuales'), words mono- or bitonal, tone changes by syntactic position; tonal minimal pairs maála/máála, mélo/mèlo. Discusses 'acento' only generically (fixed vs free accent in languages) and equates phonological tone with Spanish 'acento de intensidad'; no rule for Bubi stress placement. p. 80 exercise asks students to compare 'posición del acento' in Lingala vs Bubi words.
